7,000 YEARS
Cut open a banana,
and you will find
tiny dark specks but
no seeds that can grow.
So how does a
fruit with no working
seeds fill supermarkets
across the world?
The answer begins with
a rare accident in
the plant's chromosomes.
Wild bananas are packed
with many hard,
black seeds, each a
few millimeters across,
and very little soft flesh.
Eating one is mostly
a chore of picking out seeds.
That was the normal
pattern for wild plants
in the genus Musa
for millions of years.
Wild bananas are diploid,
with two sets of chromosomes.
Scientists think a rare
irregular cell division
in a hybrid plant
produced an egg or
pollen grain with two
sets instead of one.
When it joined a
normal one, the offspring
had three sets.
A plant with three
sets is called a triploid.
When a triploid banana
tries to make eggs
and pollen, its chromosomes
cannot pair up evenly,
because three cannot be
split into two equal groups.
The cells get mixed
up and cannot form
working seeds, so the
plant is nearly sterile.
In the wild,
that would usually be
a dead end.
But bananas have another
trick, called parthenocarpy.
The fruit can swell
and fill with soft
pulp without pollination
or fertilization.
Instead of a mouthful
of hard seeds,
there was a soft,
sweet, seedless fruit.
Rare plants like this
appeared, and people noticed.
The earliest evidence of
banana farming, from New
Guinea, is about seven
thousand years old.
So how do you
plant a banana with no seeds?
You do not need seeds.
The banana is not
a tree but a
giant herb, and underground
it has a thick
stem called a corm.
From the corm,
small shoots called suckers
keep growing, and they
are genetic copies of
the parent.
Farmers cut a sucker
away and plant it,
and within roughly a
year, it can bear fruit.
Today, many farms use
tissue culture.
Scientists take a tiny
piece of tissue from
the growing tip of
a healthy plant,
clean it, and grow
it on sterile jelly
with nutrients.
From one small piece,
thousands of identical
young plants can be grown.
So bananas do not
spread across continents
on their own.
They depend on people,
who have cloned them
for thousands of years.
And that creates a
risk we explore in
the full video.
Watch the full deep
dive on Miya's Lab
to discover the secret
of Big Mike,
the banana the world
largely lost.
